title: Regional bridgelet fallback protocol for graceful downstream degradation
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: Define and implement a lightweight regional fallback layer ("bridgelet") that allows Redwood services to degrade downstream interactions with Redis, Kafka, and mainline DBs in a controlled, observable way during partial regional failures or downstream saturation. Goal is to preserve customer-visible SLOs for high-priority requests while enabling graceful degradation for lower-priority traffic and reducing operational blast radius across regions.

Why this ticket: Recent incident (INC-2026-02-18-region-db-surge) exposed brittle downstream handling during cross-region spikes. Existing global circuit breakers are too coarse and result in total request drops or long queues; we need a finer-grained regional mechanism that composes with caching and KV prefixing to preserve correctness where possible.

Out of scope: major DB schema changes, full global quorum failover, and building a cross-region replication system. This ticket focuses on runtime routing, connection bank behavior, and graceful fallback responses for read-heavy and streaming paths.
proposal:
Design overview: introduce a "bridgelet" process colocated with regional API gateways that mediates calls to Redis/Kafka/DB. Bridgelets implement three key features:

1) Grace windows and soft circuits: replace binary open/closed circuits with time-boxed grace windows. When a downstream shows elevated latency or error rate, bridgelet transitions affected tenants into a "grace" tier where behavior is progressively degraded rather than abruptly cut. The transition is governed by SLO-weighted scoring (tenant request priority + recent error slope).

2) Ephemeral connection banks: instead of a single global connpool, bridgelet maintains small ephemeral banks per tenant-tenant-shard pair with a token-bucket soft quota. Tokens are reclaimed on request completion. Banks can be rebalanced across bridgelets using a cheap heartbeat and shadow load metric to reduce cold starts.

3) Degraded response modes and safety stubs: for reads, bridgelet can return (a) cached results from local prefix cache, (b) best-effort partial results (e.g., top-N from local shard), or (c) synthetic-but-safe responses tagged with provenance metadata so clients can opt-in to degraded reads. For write/commit paths the bridgelet enqueues to a durable local journal with backpressure signals to upstream.

Circuit bloom: to avoid expensive global coordination we use a probabilistic per-key "circuit bloom" that estimates whether a given key is currently suffering downstream failure. This enables per-key decisions to serve from cache or fall back without per-request central lookups.

Routing and SLO integration: routing policy is configurable by release and project: latency-SLO focused routes prefer partial reads and cache fallback; throughput-SLO focused routes prefer queuing and retry. Bridgelet emits SLO scores to the Console for per-route dashboarding.

Trade-offs: bridgelets add operational complexity and another moving piece to deploy. Probabilistic bloom may incur false positives causing slightly more caching than necessary; we accepted that in exchange for lower coordination overhead and faster local decisions.
acceptance_criteria: Bridgelet process can be deployed behind a feature flag in two regions simultaneously
Per-tenant ephemeral bank limits configurable and default to 20 tokens; loans returned correctly under normal load
Fallback read modes return cache or partial results with provenance header 'X-Bridgelet-Degraded: true' for 95% of targeted degrade scenarios in chaos test
End-to-end P95 latency for priority-tier requests does not regress by more than 10% in synthetic regional degradation tests
Dashboard shows per-region circuit bloom hit rate, token bank exhaustion rate, and degrade-rate per route
Automated rollback removes bridgelet routing in <5 minutes if health checks fail
rollout_plan: Phase 0: Implement bridgelet binary and local integration tests (feature-flag gated)
Phase 1: Canary deploy in a single non-prod region; run synthetic downstream-saturation scenarios
Phase 2: Enable in one production region for low-risk customer lanes (internal tenants), monitor for 72h
Phase 3: Gradually expand to more regions and increase tenant coverage; enable read-only degrade modes for broad traffic
Phase 4: Promote to default with runtime config knobs and runbook published
test_plan: Unit tests for token-bank accounting, circuit bloom insert/lookup, and fallback selection logic
Integration tests with redis-stub and kafka-stub to simulate partial availability and latency spikes
Chaos test: kill <50% of DB pods in region and verify bridgelet degrades non-priority traffic while preserving priority SLOs
Load test: burst 10x RPS with bounded downstream capacity and measure token exhaustion, queue lengths, and derived cost metrics
End-to-end regression: run eval prompts to ensure generation correctness not impacted by degraded read modes
monitoring_and_alerts: Console dashboard: bridgelet per-region degrade rate, per-route SLO score, token bank exhaustion rate
Pager alert: bridgelet health < 3/4 replicas healthy for 5m
Warning alert: token bank exhaustion > 5% for priority tenants for 10m
SLO alert integration: when observed availability for priority-route < 99.9% for 10m, trigger incident workflow
rollback_plan: Disable bridgelet routing via runtime feature flag (automatable)
Revert to direct downstream routing and enable temporary global shedder with conservative thresholds
If issue persists, scale down bridgelet and revert bridgelet configs to defaults, notify platform on-call
